Cons:
45 mm³/s limits throughput vs UHF variants
PT1000 requires firmware configuration adjustment
Priced identically to the UHF — harder to justify unless flow is not the bottleneck
Description: The Rapido 2 Plus HF is the high-temperature version of the standard-flow Rapido 2. With a 350°C ceiling and PT1000 thermistor, it unlocks PA-CF, PC, and PEI printing without stepping up to the UHF flow rate. It's the right choice for enclosed builds where high-temp materials are a regular part of the workflow.
Verdict Label: The serious-material upgrade — same HF flow, but 350°C and PT1000 for PA, PC, and composites.
Body:
The Plus variants exist for one reason: high-temperature materials. If PA-CF, PC, or PEI are in your filament rotation, the 290°C ceiling on the standard Rapido 2 will eventually become a problem. The Plus HF removes that ceiling at 350°C.

The PT1000 thermistor is the other meaningful upgrade. Above 280°C, NTC100K thermistors lose accuracy. The PT1000 keeps precise temperature readings across the full range, which matters when you're running PA-CF at 300°C in an enclosed chamber.

At 45 mm³/s, the HF flow rate is appropriate for these materials — PA-CF and PC rarely benefit from extreme throughput anyway. For builders whose priority is material versatility over print speed, the Plus HF is the most targeted choice in the lineup.
Name: Rapido 2 Plus HF
Pros:
350°C ceiling opens PA-CF, PC, PEI
PT1000 thermistor is more accurate above 280°C
Same toolhead compatibility as standard Rapido 2
Only $10 more than the HF
Ideal for enclosed builds running high-temp materials

Cons:
Premium price at $109
PT1000 requires firmware configuration
Overkill for builders who don't push high-temp exotic materials at speed
Description: The Rapido 2 Plus UHF combines the 75 mm³/s flow ceiling of the UHF with the 350°C max temperature and PT1000 thermistor of the Plus lineup. It's the no-compromise option for builders running PA-CF or PC at high speeds in enclosed chambers.
Verdict Label: The top of the Rapido 2 lineup — maximum flow AND maximum temperature for no-compromise builds.
Body:
The Rapido 2 Plus UHF is the flagship of the lineup — the only Rapido 2 variant that combines 75 mm³/s flow with a 350°C ceiling and PT1000 thermistor. For most builders, it's more hotend than they need. For the right build, it's exactly right.

Who needs it: builders running PA-CF and PC at speed in an enclosed, chambered machine. At 75 mm³/s with 350°C available, there's no material or throughput scenario in FDM prosumer printing that this hotend can't handle.

The $109 price is the highest in the lineup but reasonable given what's on offer. The main consideration is whether you'll actually use the 350°C ceiling — if your material stack tops out at ABS or ASA, the standard UHF at $99 is a better value. But if your build is spec'd around performance materials from the start, the Plus UHF is the correct answer.
Name: Rapido 2 Plus UHF
Pros:
75 mm³/s — highest flow in the Rapido 2 family
350°C ceiling for all exotic materials
PT1000 for accurate high-temp readings
Full toolhead ecosystem compatibility
Best pick for speed-focused enclosed builds

Cons:
36 mm³/s is the lowest flow in the family — noticeably limiting at high speeds
Not well-suited for large-volume production printing
PT1000 config required
Flow ceiling becomes the bottleneck before other system limits
Description: The Rapido 2F is the compact, lightweight member of the Rapido 2 family. At 36 mm³/s it has the lowest flow ceiling of the five variants, but it pairs a 350°C max temperature with PT1000 accuracy in a form factor optimized for weight-sensitive toolhead designs.
Verdict Label: A compact, high-temp option for weight-sensitive builds — but the flow ceiling is real.
Body:
The Rapido 2F is the outlier in the lineup — it trades flow ceiling for a smaller, lighter package. At 58g versus 75g for the other variants, it's designed for toolheads where mass is a meaningful concern for input shaper resonance or print quality at acceleration.

The 36 mm³/s flow ceiling is real and limiting. At anything above moderate print speeds, the 2F will be your bottleneck before your motion system is. That makes it a poor choice for production-oriented builds or anyone printing large objects regularly.

Where it earns its keep: compact toolhead designs, bowden setups, or builders who want 350°C capability and PT1000 accuracy in a stripped-down package at the lowest price in the family. At $75, it's also the entry point if you want the Plus thermal spec without paying Plus prices — the flow trade-off is the only thing standing between you and the rest of the lineup.
Name: Rapido 2F
Pros:
350°C ceiling with PT1000 for exotic materials
Most compact form factor in the Rapido 2 family
Lightest weight — benefits high-acceleration toolheads
Lowest price in the lineup at $75
Good fit for bowden or light-duty direct drive setups

Cons:
290°C ceiling rules out PA, PC without the Plus
NTC100K thermistor less accurate at high temps
Not ideal if you regularly print exotic materials
Description: The Rapido 2 HF is the standard-flow variant of Phaetus's second-generation hotend. It handles PLA, PETG, ABS, and ASA with ease at flows up to 45 mm³/s. For builders who don't need the extreme throughput of the UHF variant, the HF offers the same build quality and toolhead compatibility at a lower price.
Verdict Label: The baseline Rapido 2 — reliable, well-supported, and a proven workhorse for standard printing.
Body:
The Rapido 2 HF sits at the entry point of the Rapido 2 family, and that's not a knock — it's a strong foundation. At 45 mm³/s, it comfortably handles everything from PLA to ABS without the flow ceiling becoming a bottleneck in normal use.

Where the HF earns its place is in reliability and ecosystem fit. The NTC100K thermistor is what most Klipper configurations expect, so setup is straightforward. Stealthburner, XOL, Dragon Burner — all compatible out of the box.

The 290°C ceiling is the only real limitation. Builders who regularly print PA-CF, PC, or other high-temp materials should step up to the Plus HF. For everyone else — PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, flexible filaments — the HF is the sensible choice and leaves money on the table for the rest of your build.
Name: Rapido 2 HF
Pros:
Excellent flow for standard filaments
Well-documented community support
Compatible with all major Voron toolheads
Affordable entry into the Rapido 2 family
PT100 upgrade available via Plus variant

Cons: 290°C limit rules out high-temp engineering filaments, NTC100K not ideal for high-temp use, UHF nozzle ecosystem less universal than V6, Heater wattage inconsistently reported
Description: The Rapido 2 UHF is the ultra-high-flow variant of the Rapido 2, with a volcano-style extended melt zone pushing up to 75 mm³/s. Same titanium heat break and plated copper block as the HF, same 290°C ceiling. The go-to hotend for builders running 150mm/s and above on Voron and RatRig platforms. Prices vary by vendor — expect $99–$120 USD from North American distributors.
Verdict Label: The high-flow standard for CoreXY builds — 75 mm³/s ceiling with broad toolhead support.
Body:
The Rapido 2 UHF is not the hotend for every Voron build. If you're printing structural parts in PLA at 80mm/s, a Dragon HF does the same job for $30 less and weighs half as much. The UHF's extended melt zone and 80W heater only justify themselves once you start pushing volumetric throughput — which, on a well tuned Voron 2.4, happens above about 60mm/s with a 0.4mm nozzle.

Where the Rapido 2 UHF shines is in multi-material printing and draft mode. With a 0.6mm or 0.8mm nozzle at 200mm/s, the UHF stays well inside its thermal limits while a standard hotend is already gasping. The 80mm³/s rating means your slicer's speed limit is your motion system, not your hotend, and that's exactly the relationship you want.

The bi-metal heat break is worth mentioning independently. It outperforms titanium-only heat breaks at the top of the temperature range because it manages heat distribution more actively rather than simply insulating. For anyone printing nylon or ABS at 270°C+, the more active thermal management reduces the likelihood of partial melts creeping up the heat break.
Nozzle Thread: M6 Volcano (UHF) / M6 V6 via adapter
Name: Rapido 2 UHF
Pros: 75 mm³/s max flow, Detachable thermistor, Titanium heat break, Plated copper heat block, Includes V6 and Volcano nozzles, Wide toolhead compatibility

Cons:
Conduction cooling requires printer frame/mount to act as heatsink — not universally supported
Smaller community than established brands
More complex thermal setup than air-cooled variants
Fewer validated toolhead mounts available
Description: The Chube Conduction is the flagship of the Chube lineup, using thermal conduction through the mount structure to cool the hotend rather than a dedicated fan. This allows a longer 52mm meltzone and the highest flow rate in the family. It targets builders running enclosed, high-chamber-temp setups where fan-based cooling is a liability.
Verdict Label: The highest-flow Chube variant — conduction cooling removes the fan bottleneck entirely.
Body:
The Conduction variant is where Chube's design philosophy gets most ambitious. By removing the fan and relying on thermal conduction through the mounting hardware, it eliminates one of the consistent failure points in high-chamber-temp builds: the hotend cooling fan.

In an enclosed printer running 60–70°C chamber temps, fan-cooled hotends work harder and can develop heat creep issues at sustained high flow. The Conduction sidesteps this entirely — the mount structure becomes the heatsink. The tradeoff is that this only works if your toolhead and mount are designed to conduct heat away efficiently, which limits compatible configurations compared to the Air variant.

At 52mm meltzone and support for up to 47.5mm heater cartridges (higher wattage options), the Conduction has the highest theoretical flow ceiling in the Chube lineup. For the right enclosed build — Voron 2.4 or Trident with a properly spec'd toolhead — it's a genuinely interesting alternative to water cooling.
Name: Chube Conduction
Pros:
Conduction cooling eliminates fan dependency
Highest flow ceiling in the Chube lineup
500°C max temp
V6 nozzle compatibility
M3 hardware throughout
52mm meltzone — longest in the family
Up to 47.5mm heater cartridge support for higher wattage

Cons:
Nichrome wire heater requires careful routing and bending
Fan not included — requires separate sourcing and mounting
Silicone sock only rated to 300°C — must be removed for high-temp use
M3 thermistor thread strips easily if overtightened
Smaller reseller network than Phaetus
Setup is more involved than cartridge-heater hotends
Description: The Goliath is a high-flow hotend designed by the VzBoT team and manufactured by Mellow. It features a 50mm meltzone, nickel-plated copper heat block with a 100W 24V nichrome wire heater, and a bi-material copper-zirconia heatbreak. Mounting pattern matches the Dragon hotend, giving it broad toolhead compatibility.
Verdict Label: A VzBoT-designed extreme-flow hotend — unmatched meltzone at this price, but not a beginner install.
Body:
The Goliath is the hotend the VzBoT team built because nothing else was fast enough for their printer. A 50mm meltzone paired with a 100W nichrome heater and a 550°C ceiling puts it in a different category than anything Phaetus or E3D offers at this price point. On AliExpress it regularly lands under $35.

The Dragon-compatible mount pattern is the key to its wide adoption. It drops into Stealthburner, XOL, Dragon Burner, and most toolheads with minimal modification. That's a significant advantage for a hotend with this kind of spec.

The installation experience is less polished than a Rapido 2. The nichrome wire needs to be routed and bent carefully — do it wrong and the wire fatigues and breaks. The PT1000 M3 thread strips easily if you overtighten. The fan is not included and needs to be sourced and mounted separately. These are manageable for an experienced builder but worth knowing before you order.

For VzBoT users it's the obvious choice. For Voron builders willing to do the setup work, it's one of the best value high-flow options available.
Name: Goliath Air
Pros:
50mm meltzone — longest in any air-cooled prosumer hotend
550°C maximum temp ceiling
100W 24V nichrome heater for fast ramp times
Dragon-compatible mounting pattern — broad toolhead support
V6 nozzle thread
Bi-material copper-zirconia heatbreak
Open-source design by VzBoT team

Cons:
Requires a full water cooling loop — significant added complexity and cost
Nichrome wire routing still requires care
Silicone sock only rated to 300°C
M3 thermistor thread strips easily
Not practical for most standard Voron builds without significant modification
Description: The Goliath Water is the liquid-cooled variant of the VzBoT Goliath, replacing the air-cooled aluminum heatsink with a water-cooled block and included fittings. All other specs are identical to the Air variant. It enables sustained extreme flow rates that air cooling cannot support at prolonged high speeds.
Verdict Label: The water-cooled Goliath unlocks the full meltzone potential — for builds already running liquid cooling.
Body:
The Goliath Water is the same hotend as the Air variant with the heatsink swapped out for a water block and fittings. Everything else — meltzone, heater, heatbreak, nozzle thread, mount pattern — is identical.

The reason to choose it over the Air is sustained high-speed printing. Air cooling works until chamber temps climb or print speeds push sustained flow rates past what the heatsink can dissipate. Water cooling removes that ceiling. For VzBoT builds or any printer already running a water cooling loop, it's the natural choice.

For standard Voron builds that aren't already water-cooled, the infrastructure cost is significant. A pump, reservoir, radiator, tubing, and fittings add complexity and cost that most builders don't have headroom for. The Air variant covers the vast majority of use cases. The Water variant is for builds where it doesn't.
Name: Goliath Water
Pros:
Water cooling removes the thermal limit of air-cooled heatsink
Highest sustained flow ceiling of any listed hotend
550°C max temp
100W 24V nichrome heater
Water fittings included
Dragon-compatible mount
Open-source design

Cons:
Newer brand with smaller community footprint than Phaetus or E3D
Limited reseller network
Air cooling requires fan mounting solution not included
Fewer documented Klipper config examples
Description: The Chube Air is a high-flow, air-cooled hotend from Luke's Lab designed around V6 nozzle compatibility and all M3 hardware. With a 500°C max temp ceiling and a 42mm meltzone, it targets prosumer builders who want extreme temperature headroom without proprietary nozzle lock-in.
Verdict Label: A genuinely original high-flow design — impressive specs, but ecosystem support is still maturing.
Body:
The Chube Air makes a strong first impression on paper: 500°C ceiling, V6 nozzle compatibility, all M3 hardware, and a 42mm meltzone. For builders frustrated by proprietary nozzle systems or tiny M2.5 screws that strip on the third swap, Chube's design philosophy directly addresses real pain points.

The V6 compatibility is the most practically meaningful feature. Your existing nozzle library works. Brass, hardened, CHT variants — they all thread in. The same applies to heater cartridges and the 3x15mm thermistor sensor, which is the standard form factor most Voron builders already stock.

The gap right now is ecosystem maturity. Phaetus and E3D have years of community configs, mounting solutions, and documented quirks. Chube is newer, the reseller network is thinner, and there are fewer Klipper config examples to pull from. For early adopters willing to do some groundwork, the hardware is legitimately interesting. For builders who want a plug-and-play experience, the Rapido 2 family is still the safer bet.
Name: Chube Air
Pros:
500°C max temp — highest ceiling in its class
V6 nozzle compatibility — use your existing stock
M3 hardware throughout — no tiny screws to strip
Standard 3x15mm thermistor cartridge
6x20–22mm heater cartridge compatibility
42mm meltzone length

Cons:
45 mm³/s is the lowest flow in the Chube family
33mm meltzone is shorter than Air and Conduction
Smaller community and fewer validated configs
Not ideal for high-speed production printing
Description: The Chube Compact is the smallest member of the Chube family, with a 22.23mm OD and 48.5mm length. It uses a 6x16mm heater cartridge (upgradeable to 6x20mm) and a 33mm meltzone. Designed for toolhead designs where space and mass are a constraint but 500°C headroom is still desired.
Verdict Label: A compact V6-compatible hotend with 500°C headroom — best for weight-sensitive toolheads.
Body:
The Chube Compact occupies the same niche as the Rapido 2F — small, light, still capable of high temperatures — but with V6 nozzle compatibility as the differentiator. At 22.23mm OD it fits toolhead designs that the larger Air and Conduction variants can't.

The 33mm meltzone and 45 mm³/s ceiling are real limitations. This isn't a high-throughput hotend. But if your use case is a compact toolhead on a Voron running standard materials at moderate speed with occasional high-temp filament (PA, PC), the 500°C ceiling gives you that headroom without needing a larger body.

At $65 it's the entry point into the Chube family and the easiest to justify as a trial. If Chube's V6-native approach appeals to you, the Compact is the lowest-risk way to evaluate it before committing to the Air or Conduction variants.
Name: Chube Compact
Pros:
Smallest form factor in the Chube lineup
500°C max temp ceiling
V6 nozzle compatibility
M3 hardware throughout
Lowest price in the Chube family
22.23mm OD — drops into tight toolhead spaces
